item.text: {"question_id":"2B.8","answer":"For the 2023 period, the evidence supports a mixed and materially opaque assessment rather than a finding that military resources were wholly unrelated to security needs. Egypt faced genuine security pressures, including the Sinai insurgency, border concerns, and water-security risks; terrorist activity in Sinai declined substantially in 2023, although casualty and effectiveness data remained difficult to verify (BATCH-0006-E009; BATCH-0009-R08-E003). At the same time, military spending and procurement cannot be assessed transparently or proportionately: military-enterprise allocations were omitted from public budgets, large state-owned-enterprise audits were not public, and the military operated with broad autonomy and restricted disclosure (BATCH-0002-E005; BATCH-0008-E010; BATCH-0009-R10-E002; BATCH-0009-R10-E004). SIPRI documented substantial arms imports during 2019–2023, including combat aircraft and major warships, but those figures measure transfers rather than 2023-only decisions and do not establish corruption, unlawful intent, defensive inadequacy, or intimidation (BATCH-0011-E008). Longer-period analyses reported military-led, debt-financed megaprojects, no-bid contracting, resources directed to the military and regime-connected cronies, and substantial arms spending under Sisi’s military-centered political economy; these support concern about military-economic entrenchment and opportunity costs but do not by themselves prove that particular 2023 defense procurements were corrupt or disproportionate (BATCH-0005-E009; BATCH-0005-E010; BATCH-0009-R11-E006;
